title: Loading Data with HttpClient and httpResource
summary: Call a JSON API with HttpClient, turn the result into a signal with toSignal, declare reactive requests with httpResource and resource, and add headers with a functional interceptor.
introduction: Almost every app shows data that lives on a server. Angular ships HttpClient, a typed, testable wrapper around fetch, and since version 19 the signal-based resource APIs that re-fetch automatically when their inputs change and expose loading and error states as signals. This lesson configures the HTTP client, loads a product list both ways, reacts to a changing category, and adds an authorization header to every request.
learningObjectives: Register HttpClient with provideHttpClient and call a JSON API from a service
Convert an observable to a signal with toSignal and declare requests with httpResource
Handle loading, error and reload states and add headers with an interceptor

blocks.text: `HttpClient` is not available until you provide it. Add `provideHttpClient()` to the application configuration; `withFetch()` makes it use the browser's `fetch` API, which is also what server-side rendering needs.

blocks.title: src/app/app.config.ts

blocks.text: Keep URLs and response types in one service so components never build requests themselves. `HttpClient` methods return RxJS observables typed with the generic you pass; the JSON body is parsed for you.

blocks.title: src/app/products-api.ts

blocks.text: To display the list, convert the observable into a signal with `toSignal()`. It subscribes immediately, unsubscribes when the component is destroyed and gives the template a value to read right away, here an empty array.

blocks.title: Common mistake: a request that never happens
blocks.text: Observables are lazy. `this.api.create(product);` on its own sends nothing: no subscriber, no request. Either subscribe (`this.api.create(product).subscribe()`), convert to a promise with `await firstValueFrom(this.api.create(product))`, or hand the observable to `toSignal()`, which subscribes for you. The network tab in the browser's developer tools is the quickest way to confirm a request was really sent.

`toSignal()` is fine for a one-off load, but it cannot tell you whether the request is still running, whether it failed, or re-run when a filter changes. `httpResource()` can. You give it a function that returns the URL or a request description; Angular tracks the signals that function reads and fetches again whenever they change. The result exposes `value()`, `isLoading()`, `error()`, `status()` and a `reload()` method.

items: Changing `category` changes the request function's result, so the resource fetches again. No subscription, no `ngOnChanges`, no manual call.
`defaultValue: []` means `value()` is always an array, so the template needs no null checks. Without it, `value()` is `undefined` until the first response.
`reload()` repeats the current request, for a refresh button or after a write.
A request that is still running when its inputs change is cancelled automatically, so a slow earlier response cannot overwrite a newer one.
If the request function returns `undefined`, nothing is fetched; use that to wait until an id is known.

blocks.text: `httpResource` is for reading. Writes (POST, PUT, DELETE) stay with `HttpClient`, typically followed by `reload()` on the resource that shows the affected data.

`httpResource` is a specialised form of `resource()`, which accepts any async loader: `fetch`, a database in the browser, a WebSocket request. `params` is the reactive input and the loader receives it together with an `abortSignal` for cancellation.

rows: A single read that never changes
Not tracked; use `catchError` in the pipe
Reads that depend on signals (filters, route params)
Any async source with a custom loader

blocks.text: An interceptor is a function that sees every request before it leaves and every response before it arrives. Typical jobs: adding an `Authorization` header, logging, retrying, or redirecting to the login page on a 401. Requests are immutable, so you `clone()` them with the change.

blocks.text: A failed request produces an `HttpErrorResponse` with `status` and `message`. With `httpResource`, `error()` holds it and the template decides what to show. With observables, `catchError` from RxJS turns the failure into a fallback value or a user-facing message: `this.http.get<Product[]>(url).pipe(catchError(() => of([])))`. Show the user something in every case; a blank screen after a failed request is the most common beginner bug in data-driven pages.

blocks.title: Where is the API?
blocks.text: During development, `ng serve` can forward `/api` to a backend on another port through a proxy configuration (`ng serve --proxy-config proxy.conf.json`). That keeps the URLs in your code relative and avoids CORS errors. The [REST API tutorial](/tutorials/rest-api) covers designing the endpoints themselves.

questions.question: Calling `this.http.delete('/api/products/3')` without subscribing still sends the request.
questions.explanation: HttpClient observables are cold: nothing happens until something subscribes or the observable is converted with toSignal or firstValueFrom.

questions.question: An `httpResource` reads `this.page()` in its request function. What happens when `page` changes from 1 to 2?
questions.explanation: The request function is reactive: a change in any signal it reads triggers a new request, and the previous one is cancelled if still running.
options: A new request is sent automatically and the old one is cancelled
The resource throws because inputs cannot change
The previous value is cleared and must be re-fetched manually
